name: Dermestes marmoratus
intro: Of the four or so Dermestes species I had seen by August 2025, this was the largest. My beetles began breeding in their temporary enclosure. I photographed an adult in September. Its mottled wing covers make a good field mark to look for when checking which species has established in a box.

facts.title: Captive result
facts.text: Breeding in the holding enclosure by August 29, 2025

facts.title: Adult size
facts.text: 9–13 mm in the North American identification key

sections.title: Colony
sections.text:
I would begin with a small amount of dry animal material and leave the group together. The food history of this species gives me a better starting point than a fruit or jelly feeder. Its published records include carrion and accumulations of dead insects. I would supply a separate piece of dry material to lift when I check the box so I can find young larvae without disturbing the whole group.
My first breeding result came while the group was still in temporary housing. For that reason I check the food, loose debris and sheltered edges before moving the adults into a permanent setup. Small larvae can remain behind when the conspicuous adults have all been transferred. I keep this colony separate from the dry insects in my specimen collection.

sections.title: Adults
sections.text: Under good light I look for a marbled pattern of dark and pale hairs on the wing covers. A paler band extends inward from behind each shoulder. Several North American Dermestes are mottled, so I use the identification key when starting with new field material. The September photograph shows the appearance of my own adult.

sources.title: Biggs, Herrmann and Cognato (2022), diagnosis and natural history

gallery.caption: Adult marbled hide beetle in September 2025.
gallery.alt: A small dark Dermestes marmoratus with a mottled pattern of pale markings rests on an open palm.

gallery.caption: Temporary enclosure where the beetles bred in August 2025.
gallery.alt: A clear rearing cup holding folded white paper, a dark layer at the bottom and small beetles.

distribution.caption: Biggs and colleagues report records in Canada and the United States, including the western interior, the Gulf states and New Brunswick.
distribution.alt: Documented regions for Dermestes marmoratus: Alabama, Alberta, British Columbia, California, Colorado, Idaho, Kansas, Manitoba, Mississippi, Montana, Nevada, New Brunswick, New Mexico, North Dakota, Oklahoma, Oregon, Saskatchewan, South Dakota, Texas, Utah, Washington, Wyoming.
